# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

founder.order_why: The window screen (4) sits between two screens with the same 'define where this idea applies' prompt (3 and 5), so the context is split by a detour instead of being set in one go before the window is chosen.

founder.missing: Nothing asks about the glasses themselves or the price: no solution step (captions in the lenses, needing a phone that is with them and online), no question on who pays (the wearer, HSA/FSA) or on today's spend against $599 to $839 a year, before the study goes to people. PRIMARY.order_why: It moves sensibly from whether I talk with hearing people, to whether and how often I lost the thread, to what I'd want easier, to how my current tools did; only the counter showing '1 of 4' twice looked off.
PRIMARY.missing: Where it happened, like a noisy restaurant, a group at work or a family dinner, and whether it was too fast or too noisy. What I actually did when I lost the thread, like asking people to repeat, lipreading, bluffing, or using a captioning app or interpreter. The last question also assumes I use hearing aids or phone captions and doesn't ask what else I use.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Holding up' sits right beside '7 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', so I can see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows seven 'for' cells on a 0 to 7 axis with the marker at 6 labelled 'your bar · 6 of 7 (at least 8 in 10)', so what is counted, over how many, and where the bar sits are all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Lost the thread of a conversation with hearing people' is my problem in my words, but I never saw an 'at least 8 in 10' prevalence belief among the ones I checked; I checked importance and current-solution satisfaction, so this belief is recognisable rather than one I signed off.
screens.why_b4: 'How often, and whether it matters, are the next two cards' sends me onward but does not say what an all-yes prevalence means for the idea, such as that the wedge is real and the open question is frequency, which the stage page already flagged as disputed.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible, 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is said outright, and the So line limits the claim to 'among these 7' without calling it strong.
screens.instead: All 7 lost the thread this week, which clears your 6-of-7 bar, but 7 is a lean, not proof. The real test is whether it happens often enough to matter, and the Frequency card is where people disagree, so read that next.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'People disagree' sits right beside the number that decides it: 4 of 7 in my band against a bar of 5 of 7, 1 short, so I know it missed by one person and why.
screens.why_b2: Days out of 7 and my bar at 5 of 7 are plain, but the legend runs together as 'what you said at what you said short of it' and 'median' sits between 4 and 5, so I need a second look to see which steps are mine and where the 7 people fall.
screens.why_b3: The name Frequency and '4 to 7 days out of 7' are my numbers, but 'lose the thread of a conversation' is Keel's wording for my 'too fast or too noisy to follow', and the asked line's trailing '— the most recent time it happened' doesn't fit a count-of-days question.
screens.why_b4: 'Whether it matters is the next card' points me onward but doesn't say what this means for the idea, for example that my 4-to-7 band is too high and 2 to 3 days a week is the honest floor for most of my wearers.
screens.why_b5: n is visible as 7 answered and 7 counted, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and a one-short split is not dressed up as either a hold or a failure.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 lose the thread 4+ days a week, 1 short of your bar; the other 3 lose it on fewer days, so your band may be set too high. With 7 people it is a lean: consider whether 2 to 3 days a week still justifies the glasses, then see Importance next.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes clear the bars count 14 picks from 7 people, and the bar sits at 5 of 7, but the strip says for 7 and against 7 when every one of the 7 people counted for me, so I had to stop and work out that the against cells are the other picks rather than people.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the line about losing the thread around the table among five hard things are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line usefully says this puts it in the top two rather than first, but it never says what that means for the glasses, such as that the table is the right wedge to lead with or that I should check whether it outranks getting a word in.
screens.why_b5: The n of 7 stays visible, the small group is called a lean and not a call, and the So line refuses to stretch top two into ranks first.
screens.instead: Strip: one cell per person, all 7 for you, with the other picks shown only in the bars; So: losing the thread at the table is in everyone's top two here, so leading with group conversation fits, but with 7 people that is a lean, so check with more people whether it ranks above getting a word in.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7", so the verdict and the deciding number agree and are read together.
screens.why_b2: Each answer row carries its count and its for or against mark, the line sits under "Missed a little, caught up quickly", and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5 of 7, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title "Current solution" and the belief about hearing aids or phone captions still falling short match word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Your solution is judged against this gap on the next study" points forward, but it does not say what the gap means for AirCaps, for example that most people catch the gist and lose the details, so the captions have to win on detail.
screens.why_b5: n = 7 is visible throughout, "a small group: a lean, not a call" tempers the 6 of 7, and nothing claims more than these seven people said.
screens.instead: Today's way falls short for 6 of 7 (a lean): half catch the gist and lose the details, half lose the thread and nod along. The glasses have to give back the details, not just the gist; test that next.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Holding up' with '6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7' right beside it, so the verdict and its deciding number sit together.
screens.why_b3: The dimension name 'Current solution' and the belief line are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what Tomás's workaround means for AirCaps, for example whether people with one-sided loss are a weaker wedge than people deaf in both ears.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay honest (1 against, 1 asked), but the heading 'When a line fails' sits over a line that held, which reads as a soft misframing.
screens.why_b6: Tomás's end-seat trick shows that people deaf in one ear can manage group talk by seating themselves, a workaround and a softer sub-segment I did not type.
screens.instead: Current solution held, 6 of 7 (bar 5). The one who copes, deaf on one side only, manages by sitting at the end of the table. People with one-sided hearing loss may need the glasses less, so weight the wedge toward people deaf in both ears.

screens.why1: It is the first screen and checks whether I belong in the study, and talking with hearing people is the heart of my week, so it is obvious why it comes first.
screens.why2: Hearing people is how deaf and hard-of-hearing people like me talk about everyone else, so I can answer it at once.
screens.why3: I know whether I talked with hearing people this week: at work, at the shop, with my family.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the whole answer to a gate question, and a gate has no escape, so nothing is missing.
screens.why5: It drops 'face to face', so a week of texting or emailing hearing people would also count as yes, and it says 'every week' where the kicker says 'a recent time'.
screens.why6: The question says well, but 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is stiff for a yes-or-no question, where the guidelines say a screener ends with just 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with hearing people? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to ask whether I actually lost the thread with them this week before asking for the story.
screens.why2: 'Lose the thread' is exactly how I'd describe it, and 'hearing people' is the everyday word in my world, so I could answer at once.
screens.why3: I know whether I lost track of a conversation at work, at the shop or at dinner this week; it's my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a gate shouldn't carry escapes at all, and here there are two, one of them the banned 'I'd rather not say' and the other a long half-sentence about one particular conversation.
screens.why5: 'Lose the thread' keeps the founder's 'too fast or too noisy to follow' in plain terms, and nothing about a product or company slips through.
screens.why6: Short, one question, then 'Yes or no.' I'd hear it once and answer.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose the thread of a conversation with hearing people? Yes · No (no escape chips on this gate)

screens.why1: I just said yes, I lost the thread this week, so asking how many days that happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Losing the thread is exactly how I'd describe it when the talk runs ahead of me, and 'on how many days' is clear the first time I read or hear it.
screens.why3: I can count back over my week: the noisy lunch, the meeting where everyone talked over each other, the shop counter, and say roughly how many days it happened.
screens.why4: One to seven covers every possible count after a yes, none overlap, and 'I can't recall' fits a week that blurs together.
screens.why5: It is about following a conversation with hearing people and nothing about a product or the founder's plans reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question, then 'say a number from 1 to 7' instead of reading out seven options, then the one escape, which I could follow on one hearing, especially with the words on screen.

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I lost the thread, asking which part I'd most like made easier is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the options mix forms, so 'not being worn out by listening' and 'losing the thread' read oddly as things to make easier and I had to read them twice.
screens.why3: Every one of these happened to me in a normal week, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: 'Losing the thread around the table' overlaps with the screen's whole topic and with being worn out, and it is phrased as the problem while the others are the task, but nothing true is missing.
screens.why5: It stays on following and joining conversations with hearing people, with nothing about a product or the founder's terms reaching me.
screens.why6: Five options can be held, but they are not parallel when heard, and 'not being worn out by listening' is a negative that is awkward to hear as something to make easier.
screens.instead: Think of your last week of talking with hearing people. Which one would you most like made easier? Following talk around a table; Hearing announcements in shops and stations; Following phone and video calls; Getting a word in at the right moment; Staying less tired from listening. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After picking what I'd most like made easier, asking how my last conversation actually went with what I use now is the natural next step.
screens.why2: It assumes I used hearing aids or phone captions and lumps the two together, so I'd stop and wonder what to answer if I lipread or used neither.
screens.why3: I know how my last conversation went, but if I wasn't using hearing aids or captions that time I'd be guessing to fit the question.
screens.why4: The five steps from following everything to not following at all are in words I'd use, but 'lost the thread and mostly nodded along' and 'could not follow it at all' sit close, and there's no option for not using either tool.
screens.why5: Naming hearing aids or phone captions as the current way drifts a little from the founder's 'follow and join a conversation', and nothing asks about joining in.
screens.why6: It says well as a list of five short options, but 'following the conversation with hearing aids or phone captions' is a mouthful heard once and joins two tools with 'or'.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. How much of it did you follow? Followed nearly everything; missed a little, caught up quickly; caught the gist, missed details; lost the thread, nodded along; could not follow it. Or say you can't recall.
